warmup.q: data class Menu(val id: String, val dishes: List<String>). You build Menu("week-7", dishes) from a MutableList holding soup, and later the caller runs dishes += "pie". What does menu.dishes show?
options: [soup, pie], because the menu holds the same list
It doesn't compile: a MutableList can't be passed as a List
warmup.why: val only stops the property from pointing at another list, and List only stops writes made through that reference. The menu and the caller hold the same ArrayList, so the caller's change shows up in the menu. A MutableList is a List, so passing it compiles. Copy at the boundary (dishes.toList()) to take a snapshot.

opening:
Picture a printed recipe book. Nobody edits the page for lemon cake. When the publisher improves the recipe, a new edition comes out, and the copy on your shelf still says what it always said. Now picture the recipe card on the fridge door that the whole household scribbles on. You can never be sure which version you cooked last time.

Data in a program can be either one. A value that never changes can be shared, kept and compared without a second thought. The trap is that Kotlin code can look printed when it isn't: a val and a read-only List feel frozen, while a list someone else still holds changes underneath.

All track long, the recipe card decided and the cook did the errands, and the last lesson made failures into values too.

In this last lesson, we'll see what val, List and copy() really promise, make new editions cheaply, recurse without running out of stack, and split a whole shopping job into a pure core and a thin shell. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a printed recipe book and a fridge card everyone scribbles on. val and List turned out to be a shop window, copy() staples one page to two cards, and persistent collections print new editions that share pages. Then the track met in one job: a pure core that decides and a thin shell for the errands.

Look in your code for a function that reads the clock or a store and also decides something. Pass those values in, and the decision becomes testable.

That ends this track. Next, we'll turn to design patterns, the named designs programmers reuse. Which of them does a modern language make simpler, starting with the one that allows a single instance?

sections.h: Read-only is not immutable: what val and List really promise
sections.html:
Here's the app's weekly menu. The planner screen builds a Menu from the list of dishes the cook is editing, saves it, and then clears the list for next week:

Java
record Menu(String id, List<String> dishes) {}

Menu menu = new Menu("week-7", editing);   // editing is the screen's ArrayList
saved.add(menu);
editing.clear();                           // menu.dishes() is now empty too
Kotlin
data class Menu(val id: String, val dishes: List<String>)

val menu = Menu("week-7", editing)        // editing is the screen's MutableList
saved.add(menu)
editing.clear()                           // menu.dishes is now empty too

Everything in Menu looks printed: a data class, val properties, a read-only List. But val only means the property can't point at a different list. List only means you can't call add through that reference. Neither one freezes the object behind them, and here both sides hold the same ArrayList. A read-only List is a shop window: you can't touch the cakes, but the baker behind the glass can.

The Kotlin docs put it plainly: a read-only interface "prevents accidental modification through that interface. By contrast, an immutable collection doesn't allow you to change its elements after creation." And the read-only part is checked only at compile time. On the JVM, listOf("soup", "pie") is a java.util.Arrays$ArrayList; cast it to MutableList and set(0, "stew") works, while add throws UnsupportedOperationException.

Data classes add two traps of their own. copy() is shallow: in the docs' words, "it doesn't copy components recursively". A shallow copy is a new object whose properties point at the same objects as the original's. card.copy(recipe = "waffles") makes a new card but staples the same page of notes to both, so a note added through the copy shows up on the original too.

And equals compares every property with its own equals. For BigDecimal, Java's exact decimal number, that includes the scale, the count of digits after the point. Price("butter", BigDecimal("2.50")) == Price("butter", BigDecimal("2.5")) is false, although compareTo says the amounts are equal. Read 2.5 from one shop's website, compute 2.50 yourself, and your "same price as last week?" check says no:

Java
BigDecimal price = new BigDecimal(text).setScale(2, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY);   // same fix
Kotlin
val price = BigDecimal(text).setScale(2, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY)   // one scale for every price

UNNECESSARY throws if rounding would be needed, so a third decimal fails loudly instead of being rounded away. Storing prices as a whole number of cents avoids the question entirely.

So an immutable value, one nobody can change after it's built, needs three layers. Its properties are val. Their types are immutable all the way down: String, BigDecimal, LocalDate, other immutable data classes, immutable collections. And nothing mutable leaks in or out, which at a boundary means a copy: toList() for a snapshot, or toImmutableList() from the next section when you want the type to promise it.

val and List stop you from changing a value, not everyone else. Copy at the boundary.

Copying at every change is the price of a printed page. The next section makes that price small.

steps: Read ReadOnly.kt and predict each of the five numbered lines before you run it.
Run it, then run ReadOnlyJava.java, where List.copyOf takes a real snapshot.

code.title: ReadOnly.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l08.demo import java.math.BigDecimal data class Menu(val id: String, val dishes: List<String>) data class Price(val item: String, val amount: BigDecimal) data class Card(val recipe: String, val notes: MutableList<String>) fun main() { // 1. a read-only List can be a view of a list someone else still changes val backing = mutableListOf("soup") val menu = Menu("week-7", backing) backing += "pie" println("1. menu after the caller adds pie: ${menu.dishes}") // 2. read-only is a compile-time view: a cast gets around it (menu.dishes as MutableList<String>) += "cake" println("2. after a cast and an add: ${menu.dishes}") // 3. listOf gives a fixed-size view of an array on the JVM val fixed = listOf("soup", "pie") println("3. listOf's class: ${fixed.javaClass.name}") (fixed as MutableList<String>)[0] = "stew" println(" after set(0, \"stew\"): $fixed") try { fixed.add("cake") } catch (e: UnsupportedOperationException) { println(" add: UnsupportedOperationException") } // 4. copy() is shallow: both copies share one list val a = Card("pancakes", mutableListOf("use buttermilk")) val b = a.copy(recipe = "waffles") b.notes += "double the sugar" println("4. a.notes = ${a.notes}, same list: ${a.notes === b.notes}") // 5. BigDecimal.equals compares the scale too, and data class equals uses it println("5. Price(2.50) == Price(2.5): ${Price("butter", BigDecimal("2.50")) == Price("butter", BigDecimal("2.5"))}") println(" compareTo says equal: ${BigDecimal("2.50").compareTo(BigDecimal("2.5")) == 0}") }

alt.title: ReadOnlyJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l08.demo; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; /** The same traps in Java: views that change, and BigDecimal.equals inside a record. */ public class ReadOnlyJava { record Menu(String id, List<String> dishes) {} record Price(String item, BigDecimal amount) {} public static void main(String[] args) { // 1. a record holding the caller's list sees every later change List<String> backing = new ArrayList<>(List.of("soup")); Menu menu = new Menu("week-7", backing); backing.add("pie"); System.out.println("1. menu after the caller adds pie: " + menu.dishes()); // 2. Collections.unmodifiableList is a view too: it blocks writes through it, not changes behind it List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(backing); backing.add("cake"); System.out.println("2. unmodifiable view: " + view); // 3. List.copyOf takes a real snapshot (JDK 10+) and rejects writes Menu safe = new Menu("week-8", List.copyOf(backing)); backing.add("tart"); System.out.println("3. snapshot after another add: " + safe.dishes()); try { safe.dishes().add("jam"); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println(" add: UnsupportedOperationException"); } // 4. BigDecimal.equals compares the scale, and record equals uses it System.out.println("4. Price(2.50).equals(Price(2.5)): " + new Price("butter", new BigDecimal("2.50")).equals(new Price("butter", new BigDecimal("2.5")))); System.out.println(" compareTo says equal: " + (new BigDecimal("2.50").compareTo(new BigDecimal("2.5")) == 0)); } }

try.expect: Line 1 shows [soup, pie]: the menu sees the caller's add. Line 2 shows [soup, pie, cake]: a cast gets past the read-only type. listOf is a java.util.Arrays$ArrayList, so set works and add throws. copy() shares the notes (same list: true), and Price(2.50) == Price(2.5) is false while compareTo says equal. Java's Collections.unmodifiableList is only a view too, but List.copyOf is a snapshot. With toList(), line 1 shows [soup]: the menu has its own snapshot. Line 2 now throws UnsupportedOperationException, but only by luck: for one element, toList() returns java.util.Collections$SingletonList. From two elements up it returns a plain ArrayList, and the cast-and-add would work. The read-only type is the only promise you get.

sections.h: Persistent collections: a new edition instead of crossing out
sections.html:
Immutable values pay you back in three ways. You can share them between threads (paths of work that run at the same time) with no lock, because nobody can write ("Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal" in the first track). You can keep the old version, the way an old edition stays on the shelf. And a test can hold the "before" and "after" side by side. The price is that every change makes a new value. Copying a whole list to add one step is what Java does in the Try it, and it costs time and memory in proportion to the list's size, on every change.

Persistent collections avoid most of that copy. A new version shares most of its insides with the old one, the way a new edition of a cookbook reuses most of its pages and reprints only the ones that changed. Adding a step builds a few new pieces of the list's inner tree and reuses the rest. The library is kotlinx-collections-immutable, version 0.5.2 in the lab. Its README still says "the library is experimental and the API is subject to change", so treat it as a dependency that hasn't reached 1.0. ImmutableList promises that nobody can change the list; PersistentList adds the operations that return a new version:

Java
// Java equivalent: no persistent collections in the JDK, so copy the whole list per version
List<String> v1 = List.of("preheat the oven");
List<String> v2 = Stream.concat(v1.stream(), Stream.of("cream butter and sugar")).toList();
List<String> tmp = new ArrayList<>(v2);
tmp.addAll(List.of("beat in the eggs", "fold in the flour"));
List<String> v3 = List.copyOf(tmp);
Kotlin
val v1 = persistentListOf("preheat the oven")
val v2 = v1.adding("cream butter and sugar")             // a new list; v1 is untouched
val v3 = v2.addingAll(listOf("beat in the eggs", "fold in the flour"))
val v4 = v3.mutate { it.removeAt(0); it += "bake for 25 minutes" }   // several changes in one go

The picture breaks in one place. A publisher prints a whole new book, while a persistent list really does share its pages between versions, in memory. That sharing is safe only because no version can ever change.

Notice the names. Until 0.5.0 these methods were called add, remove, put and set, like the changing methods on MutableList. That invited a quiet bug: budget.entries.add(entry) as a statement builds a new list and throws it away, and the budget never changes. Version 0.5.0 renamed the copy-returning methods to adding, removing, putting, replacingAt and removingAt. It follows a naming proposal (KEEP-0459, still a draft) where a verb like add changes the object and a participle like adding returns a copy, as sorted() does next to sort(). The old names still compile, with a warning: 'fun add(element: String): PersistentList<String>' is deprecated. Use adding() instead.

A persistent collection makes a new version and leaves the old one alone. Keep the result, or the change is lost.

In the lab, the household budget book is a data class around a PersistentList<Entry>, and posting returns a new budget with copy(entries = entries.addingAll(...)). The budget you posted to is still there, unchanged, for the test to compare against.

Immutable data changes how functional code loops, too. Instead of a var that changes, a function often calls itself.

code.title: Persistent.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l08.demo import kotlinx.collections.immutable.mutate import kotlinx.collections.immutable.persistentListOf fun main() { // the steps of a recipe, one edition at a time val v1 = persistentListOf("preheat the oven") val v2 = v1.adding("cream butter and sugar") // a new list; v1 is untouched val v3 = v2.addingAll(listOf("beat in the eggs", "fold in the flour")) println("v1 = $v1") println("v2 = $v2") println("v3 = $v3") println("v1 is a ${v1.javaClass.simpleName}") // several changes at once, through a short-lived mutable builder val v4 = v3.mutate { steps -> steps.removeAt(0) steps += "bake for 25 minutes" } println("v4 = $v4") println("v3 = $v3 (unchanged)") // Uncomment the next line and run: the old name compiles with a deprecation warning, // returns a new list like adding, and here the new list is thrown away. // v1.add("lost") println("v1 = $v1 at the end") }

alt.title: PersistentJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l08.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Java equivalent: the JDK has no persistent collections. A new edition means copying the old one * (every element, on every change) into an unmodifiable list. Sharing structure needs a library. */ public class PersistentJava { static List<String> adding(List<String> list, String element) { List<String> copy = new ArrayList<>(list); // copies every element copy.add(element); return List.copyOf(copy); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> v1 = List.of("preheat the oven"); List<String> v2 = adding(v1, "cream butter and sugar"); List<String> v3 = adding(adding(v2, "beat in the eggs"), "fold in the flour"); System.out.println("v1 = " + v1); System.out.println("v2 = " + v2); System.out.println("v3 = " + v3); List<String> builder = new ArrayList<>(v3); // several changes: copy once, change, freeze builder.remove(0); builder.add("bake for 25 minutes"); List<String> v4 = List.copyOf(builder); System.out.println("v4 = " + v4); System.out.println("v3 = " + v3 + " (unchanged)"); } }

try.expect: v1 stays [preheat the oven] and v3 stays four steps long, even after v4 is built from it with mutate. v1 is a SmallPersistentVector. With v1.add("lost"), the build warns 'fun add(element: String): PersistentList<String>' is deprecated. Use adding() instead. and the last line still shows [preheat the oven]: add returned a new list that nobody kept. The Java version copies the full list for every version it makes.

sections.h: Recursion: tailrec is a loop, everything else uses the stack
sections.html:
Functional code often recurses where Java code loops: a function calls itself on a smaller problem. On the JVM that has a hard limit. Every call takes a stack frame, a slot that holds the call's local variables until it returns, on the thread's stack: the memory that holds the calls in progress. The stack has room for only so many. The JVM never removes a frame early, even for the last call in a method. Sum the numbers 1 to 1,000,000 by recursion and you get a StackOverflowError, in both languages. In Java it overflows even when the recursive call is the last thing the method does.

Kotlin's tailrec moves the fix into the compiler. "When a function is marked with the tailrec modifier and meets the required formal conditions, the compiler optimizes out the recursion, leaving behind a fast and efficient loop based version instead." A tail call is a call that is the very last thing a function does. The trick is an accumulator, an extra parameter that carries the result so far. The work still pending becomes an argument, so the recursive call can come last:

Java
// Java has no tailrec: write the loop the Kotlin compiler would write
static long sumTo(long n) {
    long acc = 0;
    while (n > 0) { acc += n; n--; }
    return acc;
}
Kotlin
tailrec fun sumTo(n: Long, acc: Long = 0): Long = if (n == 0L) acc else sumTo(n - 1, acc + n)
// sumTo(1_000_000) == 500000500000, no stack growth

javap -c, the JDK tool that prints a class's bytecode, shows what the compiler did. sumTo stores the new values into its own parameter slots and ends with goto 0, a jump back to its first instruction. There's no invokestatic sumTo left. The conditions are strict. The function must call itself as its very last operation, not inside try, catch or finally, and it can't be open. Get it wrong and the compiler takes your word for it, mutters a warning and compiles ordinary recursion anyway: A function is marked as tail-recursive but no tail calls are found. and Recursive call is not a tail call. The code still overflows, so read the warnings.

Here's recursion that fits tailrec naturally. A sourdough starter is fed from a spoonful of another starter, which came from another, and friends pass them on for years. Walking back to the very first one makes one call per generation, always as the last thing the function does, so the demo walks 100,000 generations without growing the stack.

Some recursion has no tail form. Counting the parts of a recipe made of parts, each made of more parts, makes several recursive calls per part. DeepRecursiveFunction from the standard library runs such a function with its "stack" on the heap, the big memory area where objects live, using coroutine machinery. In the Try it, it counts a recipe nested 100,001 levels deep, where the same code as a plain function overflows.

Most of the time you need neither. Adding up a basket or a budget is a fold or a sumOf (the collections lesson), which says what it means in one line and compiles to the same kind of loop. Recursion that walks a list with first() and drop(1) is worse than either, because drop(1) copies the rest of the list at every step.

Reach for fold or sumOf first. Keep tailrec for problems that are recursive by nature, and read its warnings.

We now have every piece of the track: pure functions, function values, collections, errors as values and data that can't change. The last section puts them into one shape.

try.title: Watch tailrec become a goto
steps: Run Recursion.kt. Predict which lines print a number and which print StackOverflowError.
From labs/, run javap -c -p -cp functional/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.functional.l08.demo.RecursionKt and find sumTo and sumNaive. Which one calls itself?
Add tailrec in front of fun sumNaive and run again. Read the warnings in the build output.
Run RecursionJava.java. Does sumTail, with its call in tail position, survive?

code.title: Recursion.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l08.demo /** Sums 1..n with recursion that is NOT in tail position: one stack frame per number. */ fun sumNaive(n: Long): Long = if (n == 0L) 0 else n + sumNaive(n - 1) /** The same sum with an accumulator: the recursive call is the last thing it does. */ tailrec fun sumTo(n: Long, acc: Long = 0): Long = if (n == 0L) acc else sumTo(n - 1, acc + n) /** A sourdough starter is fed from a spoonful of another starter. Walk back to the very first one. */ data class Starter(val id: String, val parentId: String?) tailrec fun originOf(id: String, byId: Map<String, Starter>): String { val parent = byId.getValue(id).parentId ?: return id return originOf(parent, byId) } /** A recipe made of parts, each part made of parts: counting them is recursion that can't be put in tail form. */ class Part(val parts: List<Part>) val countParts = DeepRecursiveFunction<Part, Long> { part -> var total = 1L for (child in part.parts) total += callRecursive(child) // the "stack" lives on the heap total } fun main() { println("tailrec sumTo(1,000,000) = ${sumTo(1_000_000)}") try { println("sumNaive(1,000,000) = ${sumNaive(1_000_000)}") } catch (e: StackOverflowError) { println("sumNaive(1,000,000): StackOverflowError") } println("fold over 1..1,000,000 = ${(1L..1_000_000L).fold(0L) { acc, n -> acc + n }}") val family = (1..100_000).associate { i -> "s$i" to Starter("s$i", if (i == 1) null else "s${i - 1}") } println("origin of s100000 = ${originOf("s100000", family)}") var deep = Part(emptyList()) repeat(100_000) { deep = Part(listOf(deep)) } // absurdly deep, to make the point println("parts in a recipe nested 100,001 levels deep = ${countParts(deep)}") }

alt.title: RecursionJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l08.demo; import java.util.stream.LongStream; /** Java has no tailrec, and the JVM doesn't remove tail calls: a call in tail position still uses a frame. */ public class RecursionJava { static long sumNaive(long n) { return n == 0 ? 0 : n + sumNaive(n - 1); } static long sumTail(long n, long acc) { return n == 0 ? acc : sumTail(n - 1, acc + n); } // tail position, still a call static long sumLoop(long n) { // what tailrec writes for you long acc = 0; while (n > 0) { acc += n; n--; } return acc; } public static void main(String[] args) { try { System.out.println("sumTail(1,000,000) = " + sumTail(1_000_000, 0)); } catch (StackOverflowError e) { System.out.println("sumTail(1,000,000): StackOverflowError"); } try { System.out.println("sumNaive(1,000,000) = " + sumNaive(1_000_000)); } catch (StackOverflowError e) { System.out.println("sumNaive(1,000,000): StackOverflowError"); } System.out.println("loop = " + sumLoop(1_000_000)); System.out.println("LongStream.sum = " + LongStream.rangeClosed(1, 1_000_000).sum()); } }

try.expect: sumTo and fold both print 500000500000; sumNaive overflows; originOf walks 100,000 starters back to s1; countParts returns 100001. In javap, sumTo ends with goto 0 and never calls itself, while sumNaive has invokestatic sumNaive. Marking sumNaive as tailrec gives A function is marked as tail-recursive but no tail calls are found. and Recursive call is not a tail call., and it still overflows. In Java, sumTail overflows too: the JVM doesn't remove tail calls, so only a loop helps.

sections.h: A functional core decides, a thin shell does the errands
sections.html:
Here's the track's last step: put the pieces into one shape. The lab's LegacyShoppingJob runs every morning in the recipe app. In one loop it reads the clock and loads the shopping list. It skips crossed-off items, holds back items it's too early to order, adds up a total per shop and works out each shop's member discount. Then it sends the orders, writes each one into the household budget book and saves the book, with println in between. It works. But to test one discount rule you need a fake store, a fake shop, a fixed clock, and checks on what the fakes recorded.

The fix is the shape from the first lesson of this track: the recipe card decides and the cook does the errands. Its usual name is functional core, imperative shell. The functional core is a pure function. It takes plain values, today's date included, and returns a value that describes what should happen:

Java
static ShoppingPlan planShopping(List<Item> items, Map<String, Shop> shops, LocalDate today)
Kotlin
fun planShopping(items: List<Item>, shops: Map<String, Shop>, today: LocalDate): ShoppingPlan

Everything from this track fits in there. filterNot, partition, groupBy and sumOf from the collections lesson do the work. Data classes of vals, with prices as BigDecimal at scale 2, carry it. Expected outcomes, like an item from a shop the app doesn't know, come back as values in the plan instead of exceptions or log lines, as the errors lesson taught.

The imperative shell is the thin outer part, the only code that touches the world, and it has almost no branches:

Java
ShoppingPlan run() {
    LocalDate today = LocalDate.now(clock);                                        // 1. read
    ShoppingPlan plan = planShopping(store.shoppingList(), store.shops(), today);  // 2. decide
    plan.orders().forEach(shopApi::send);                                          // 3. act
    store.saveBudget(posting(store.loadBudget(), plan.orders(), "shopping-" + today));
    return plan;
}
Kotlin
fun run(): ShoppingPlan {
    val today = LocalDate.now(clock)                                         // 1. read
    val plan = planShopping(store.shoppingList(), store.shops(), today)      // 2. decide
    plan.orders.forEach(shopApi::send)                                       // 3. act
    store.saveBudget(store.loadBudget().posting(plan.orders, "shopping-$today"))
    return plan
}

The tests change shape with the code. The core gets many small tests that build a list, call a function and compare the result with equals: no fakes, no clock, milliseconds each. Because the date is a parameter, "an item needed in ten days is still waiting" and "the same item is ordered three days later" are two lines. The shell gets one test with fakes that checks the wiring.

The shell isn't pure and doesn't try to be. The program still does all its errands. What moved is the decisions: each one now lives where you can test it with a value, like a recipe card you can read without lighting the oven.

Decide in the core, with every input passed in. Let the shell read, call the core and act, and nothing more.

try.title: Run a core and its shell
steps: Read CoreShell.kt. decideFridge is the core and FridgeJob is the shell. Predict the two decisions and the one reminder.
Change now to one day later, 2026-03-11T09:00:00Z. Without running anything, which decision changes? Then run it to check.

code.title: CoreShell.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l08.demo import java.time.Clock import java.time.Duration import java.time.Instant import java.time.ZoneOffset data class Leftover(val id: String, val dish: String, val cookedAt: Instant) sealed interface FridgeDecision { data class ThrowOut(val id: String) : FridgeDecision data class Keep(val id: String, val goodFor: Duration) : FridgeDecision } val KEEPS_FOR: Duration = Duration.ofDays(3) /** The core: leftovers older than three days go. Pure: the time is a parameter. */ fun decideFridge(leftovers: List<Leftover>, now: Instant): List<FridgeDecision> = leftovers.map { l -> val age = Duration.between(l.cookedAt, now) if (age >= KEEPS_FOR) FridgeDecision.ThrowOut(l.id) else FridgeDecision.Keep(l.id, KEEPS_FOR - age) } /** The shell: reads, calls the core, carries out the decisions. No rules in here. */ class FridgeJob(private val load: () -> List<Leftover>, private val remind: (String) -> Unit, private val clock: Clock) { fun run() { val decisions = decideFridge(load(), clock.instant()) // read, then decide decisions.filterIsInstance<FridgeDecision.ThrowOut>().forEach { remind(it.id) } // act } } fun main() { val now = Instant.parse("2026-03-10T09:00:00Z") val leftovers = listOf( Leftover("l1", "soup", Instant.parse("2026-03-06T09:00:00Z")), // cooked 4 days before now Leftover("l2", "rice", Instant.parse("2026-03-09T03:00:00Z")), // cooked 30 hours before now ) println("core, called with plain values:") decideFridge(leftovers, now).forEach { println(" $it") } println("shell, with a fixed clock and a fake phone:") FridgeJob({ leftovers }, { println(" reminder: throw out leftover $it") }, Clock.fixed(now, ZoneOffset.UTC)).run() }

alt.title: CoreShellJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l08.demo; import java.time.Clock; import java.time.Duration; import java.time.Instant; import java.time.ZoneOffset; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Consumer; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** The same core and shell in Java: records for the values, a static method for the pure core. */ public class CoreShellJava { record Leftover(String id, String dish, Instant cookedAt) {} sealed interface FridgeDecision {} record ThrowOut(String id) implements FridgeDecision {} record Keep(String id, Duration goodFor) implements FridgeDecision {} static final Duration KEEPS_FOR = Duration.ofDays(3); /** The core: leftovers older than three days go. Pure: the time is a parameter. */ static List<FridgeDecision> decideFridge(List<Leftover> leftovers, Instant now) { return leftovers.stream().<FridgeDecision>map(l -> { Duration age = Duration.between(l.cookedAt(), now); return age.compareTo(KEEPS_FOR) >= 0 ? new ThrowOut(l.id()) : new Keep(l.id(), KEEPS_FOR.minus(age)); }).toList(); } /** The shell: reads, calls the core, carries out the decisions. */ record FridgeJob(Supplier<List<Leftover>> load, Consumer<String> remind, Clock clock) { void run() { for (FridgeDecision d : decideFridge(load.get(), clock.instant())) { if (d instanceof ThrowOut t) remind.accept(t.id()); } } } public static void main(String[] args) { Instant now = Instant.parse("2026-03-10T09:00:00Z"); List<Leftover> leftovers = List.of( new Leftover("l1", "soup", Instant.parse("2026-03-06T09:00:00Z")), // cooked 4 days before now new Leftover("l2", "rice", Instant.parse("2026-03-09T03:00:00Z"))); // cooked 30 hours before now System.out.println("core, called with plain values:"); decideFridge(leftovers, now).forEach(d -> System.out.println(" " + d)); System.out.println("shell, with a fixed clock and a fake phone:"); new FridgeJob(() -> leftovers, id -> System.out.println(" reminder: throw out leftover " + id), Clock.fixed(now, ZoneOffset.UTC)).run(); } }

try.expect: The core prints ThrowOut(id=l1) (4 days old) and Keep(id=l2, goodFor=PT42H) (30 hours old, 42 hours left). The shell sends one reminder: reminder: throw out leftover l1. One day later, l2 is still kept with PT18H left, and l1 goes as before. You could check that from the core alone, with no clock and no phone, which is the point.

compare.title: Immutable values and a pure core: Java records vs Kotlin data classes

java.title: Shopping.java
java.html: record Order(String shopId, BigDecimal total, BigDecimal discount, BigDecimal toPay) {} record Budget(List<Entry> entries) { Budget { entries = List.copyOf(entries); } // snapshot: nobody can change it later Budget posting(List<Entry> more) { // a new version, by copying everything List<Entry> all = new ArrayList<>(entries); all.addAll(more); return new Budget(all); } } static BigDecimal discount(BigDecimal total, BigDecimal rate) { // pure: same inputs, same output return total.multiply(rate).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN); }

kotlin.title: Shopping.kt
kotlin.html: data class Order(val shopId: String, val total: BigDecimal, val discount: BigDecimal, val toPay: BigDecimal) data class Budget(val entries: PersistentList<Entry>) // the type promises it can't change fun Budget.posting(more: List<Entry>): Budget = copy(entries = entries.addingAll(more)) // a new version that shares structure fun discount(total: BigDecimal, rate: BigDecimal): BigDecimal = // pure: same inputs, same output (total * rate).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN)

compare.note: Both languages give you a value type whose equals compares contents, and in both equals uses BigDecimal.equals, so the scale counts. Kotlin's data class adds copy(), which Java records lack (you write "wither" methods by hand), and both are shallow. The real difference is in collections. Java's List.copyOf makes a snapshot that refuses changes at run time, but every new version copies the whole list. Kotlin's List is only a compile-time read-only view, so you need toList() for a snapshot, or kotlinx.collections.immutable for a real promise; its PersistentList makes new versions cheaply by sharing structure. The pure functions themselves look the same in both languages. Purity is a habit, not a keyword: neither compiler checks it.

worked.title: Pull the decisions out of a pantry check

steps.say: Each night the app checks the opened jars in the pantry. A jar past its use-by date goes; a jar within two days of it goes on the shopping list, unless it's on there already; anything else waits. Before reading on, label every line as read, decide or act.
steps.code: fun checkPantry() { for (jar in pantry.openJars()) { // read val daysLeft = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(LocalDate.now(), jar.useBy) // read (the clock!) if (daysLeft < 0) { // decide pantry.remove(jar.id) // act phone.notify("throw out the ${jar.name}") // act } else if (daysLeft <= 2 && !jar.onShoppingList) { // decide shoppingList.add(jar.name, "use within $daysLeft days") // act } } }

alt.html: void checkPantry() { for (Jar jar : pantry.openJars()) { // read long daysLeft = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(LocalDate.now(), jar.useBy()); // read (the clock!) if (daysLeft < 0) { // decide pantry.remove(jar.id()); // act phone.notify("throw out the " + jar.name()); // act } else if (daysLeft <= 2 && !jar.onShoppingList()) { // decide shoppingList.add(jar.name(), "use within " + daysLeft + " days"); // act } } }

steps.say: 1. Name the decisions as values. A sealed type makes the plan explicit and lets the shell's when be exhaustive.
steps.code: sealed interface JarAction { data class ThrowOut(val jarId: String, val name: String) : JarAction data class Restock(val jarId: String, val name: String, val daysLeft: Long) : JarAction data class Wait(val jarId: String) : JarAction }

alt.html: sealed interface JarAction {} record ThrowOut(String jarId, String name) implements JarAction {} record Restock(String jarId, String name, long daysLeft) implements JarAction {} record Wait(String jarId) implements JarAction {}

steps.say: 1. Write the core as a pure function. The clock becomes a parameter, today, and the result is a list of decisions. Every rule is now testable with one line: decide(listOf(jar), LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 10)).
steps.code: fun decide(jars: List<Jar>, today: LocalDate): List<JarAction> = jars.map { jar -> val daysLeft = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(today, jar.useBy) when { daysLeft < 0 -> JarAction.ThrowOut(jar.id, jar.name) daysLeft <= 2 && !jar.onShoppingList -> JarAction.Restock(jar.id, jar.name, daysLeft) else -> JarAction.Wait(jar.id) } }

alt.html: static List<JarAction> decide(List<Jar> jars, LocalDate today) { return jars.stream().<JarAction>map(jar -> { long daysLeft = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(today, jar.useBy()); if (daysLeft < 0) return new ThrowOut(jar.id(), jar.name()); if (daysLeft <= 2 && !jar.onShoppingList()) return new Restock(jar.id(), jar.name(), daysLeft); return new Wait(jar.id()); }).toList(); }

steps.say: 1. The shell reads, calls the core and carries out each action with an exhaustive when. It has no rules left, so one test with fakes covers it. The many rule tests go against decide with plain values.
steps.code: fun checkPantry() { val actions = decide(pantry.openJars(), LocalDate.now(clock)) // read, then decide for (action in actions) when (action) { // act is JarAction.ThrowOut -> { pantry.remove(action.jarId); phone.notify("throw out the ${action.name}") } is JarAction.Restock -> shoppingList.add(action.name, "use within ${action.daysLeft} days") is JarAction.Wait -> Unit } }

alt.html: void checkPantry() { List<JarAction> actions = decide(pantry.openJars(), LocalDate.now(clock)); // read, then decide for (JarAction action : actions) { // act switch (action) { case ThrowOut t -> { pantry.remove(t.jarId()); phone.notify("throw out the " + t.name()); } case Restock r -> shoppingList.add(r.name(), "use within " + r.daysLeft() + " days"); case Wait w -> { } } } }

lab.title: Split the shopping job into a pure core and a thin shell
steps: Run the tests. All eight fail. Seven of them call planShopping or posting with plain values: no fakes and no clock.
Read LegacyShoppingJob.run and label each line read, decide or act. Model.kt holds the types and needs no changes.
Write planShopping in ShoppingCore.kt from the rules in its KDoc. today is a parameter; don't touch a clock.
Write ShoppingJob.run as a thin shell: read, call the core, send each order, post and save the budget once, return the plan.
Run the tests until all eight pass. Then ask: which test would fail if planShopping called LocalDate.now() instead of using today?
hints: partition splits a list in two in one pass. Use it twice: first known and unknown shops, then items due today and items still waiting.
sumOf { it.price } has a BigDecimal overload. Round the discount with setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN), or the test's BigDecimal("3.64") won't equal your 3.63950.
groupBy keeps first-seen order. toSortedMap() sorts the groups by shop id.
In the shell, plan.orders.forEach(shopApi::send) and store.loadBudget().posting(plan.orders, "shopping-$today") cover steps 3 and 4.

drill.title: tailrec from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write originOf(id, byId), which follows parentId links from a sourdough starter back to the very first one, as a tailrec function. Then write the Java loop. Last, predict: what happens if you add a log.debug(...) line after the recursive call?

answer.html: tailrec fun originOf(id: String, byId: Map<String, Starter>): String { val parent = byId.getValue(id).parentId ?: return id // no parent: this is the first starter return originOf(parent, byId) // the last thing the function does } // A log line after the call makes it no longer a tail call: Kotlin warns // "Recursive call is not a tail call." and compiles ordinary recursion, which can overflow.

alt.html: static String originOf(String id, Map<String, Starter> byId) { String current = id; while (true) { String parent = byId.get(current).parentId(); if (parent == null) return current; // no parent: this is the first starter current = parent; // what tailrec's goto does } }

recap: val stops reassignment and List stops writes through that reference. Neither freezes the object: a read-only view changes when its backing list does.
copy() is shallow, and data class equals uses BigDecimal.equals, which compares the scale. Bring prices to one scale when you read them.
kotlinx.collections.immutable 0.5.2, still marked experimental, gives persistent collections: adding, putting and removingAt return new versions that share structure, and mutate { } batches changes.

tailrec turns a self-call in tail position into a goto. Anywhere else it's only a warning, and the stack still overflows. DeepRecursiveFunction handles deep recursion with no tail form, and fold is usually simplest.
A functional core decides from plain values, with the clock passed in; a thin shell reads, calls the core and does the I/O. Core tests need no fakes, and the shell needs one wiring test.
The limit: neither compiler checks any of this. Kotlin has no keyword for pure or for deeply immutable, so both stay habits, and the shell stays thin only because you keep it thin.

explain.prompt: A new teammate asks why the shopping job was split into planShopping and ShoppingJob, when the old job "worked fine". Explain what changed and how it changes the tests.
explain.answer: The old job worked, but its decisions were mixed with its I/O. It read the clock, loaded the list, applied the waiting and discount rules, sent the orders and saved the budget in one loop, so testing a single rule needed a fake store, a fake shop and a fixed clock, plus checks on what the fakes recorded. Now planShopping is a pure function: items, shops and today's date go in, and a plan comes out, with the same answer every time. All the rules live there, and each test builds a few values and compares the plan with equals, in milliseconds. A different day is just a different argument. ShoppingJob keeps only the I/O: read, call the core, send the orders, post and save the budget. It has almost no branches, so one test with fakes is enough to check the wiring. The data is immutable too, so the plan and the budget versions can't change behind our backs while we test or retry.

deeper.html:
Immutability is also a concurrency tool, and the memory model track explains why. A val property compiles to a final field, and the Java memory model gives final fields a special promise: once the constructor has finished, any thread that sees the object sees those fields fully set, without a lock, as long as the constructor didn't let this escape ("Safe publication, final fields and escaping this"). So an object whose state is all vals of immutable types can be handed to another thread with no synchronization at all. A persistent collection extends that: one thread builds a new version with adding while other threads keep reading the old one, and neither can disturb the other. The catch is the same as in the first section. A val holding a MutableList gets the promise only for the reference, not for the list's contents.

The naming change in kotlinx.collections.immutable came with a compiler feature. The 0.5.0 line builds the library itself with Kotlin's Experimental return-value checker in its strictest mode, -Xreturn-value-checker=full. The checker arrived in Kotlin 2.3.0, is off by default, and warns when a call's result is ignored. Both changes go after the same bug: a new version computed and then dropped.

On recursion, arrow-core 2.3.0 also contains a MemoizedDeepRecursiveFunction, a variant of the standard library's DeepRecursiveFunction that remembers its answers. Reach for either only after a plain fold or a loop has been ruled out.
